en: You ask, the assistant answers, and you use the answer to decide something, whether that is writing a text, sorting out a work question or understanding a contract.
One day it starts making more mistakes, answering differently or refusing what it used to do, and you have no way of knowing what changed or why.

It depends on the continuity of the system, the relative stability of the interface, the maintenance of the conditions of access, the model for presenting answers, the warnings, the contextual limits, the memory or history mechanisms where they exist, and the private rules that structure the very field of use.<1>p. 759</1>
What are you actually using?

It does not matter whether the service is called artificial intelligence, an assistant, a chat or a productivity tool. The name decides nothing. What decides is how the service works on the inside and who controls that workings over time.

And the service does not hand out loose answers, the way an encyclopedia would hand out an entry. It chooses what to say, in what order and in what tone, and in doing so it organizes the way you understand the problem that brought you to it.

You trust the answer, put it into your work, review it, correct it and ask again. That is exactly where the value of the service lies, because it does not just answer but makes you treat the answer as a good starting point for acting.

They consume a private arrangement of selection, formulation, prioritization, synthesis, interface language and presentation of answers that organizes the very experience of useful knowledge.<1>p. 758</1>
Why is this not just a program you use?

The terms of use of the major assistants themselves show that you do not receive a finished, static tool. You enter an environment governed by the company's rules, policies and guidelines, which it can change, limit and reorganize whenever it wants.

What you use depends on a lot of things that stay on the company's side. It depends on the system staying online, the screen staying similar, the conditions of access, the warnings that appear, the memory of the conversation when there is one and the internal rules of the service.
That is why the law looks at the whole service, and not only at the sentence that appeared on the screen.
In both cases, the contractual framework does not merely describe access to a static tool.<1>p. 758</1>
It describes entry into a regulated ecosystem of use, subject to conditioning, limitation and reorganization by private governance.<1>p. 758</1>
In other words, enjoyment does not reside only in the individual answer, but in the functional arrangement that makes it possible to trust, use, review and contest the service rendered.<1>p. 759</1>
Why does a wrong answer not sum up the problem?
There are two ways of looking at this conflict that seem reasonable but miss the target.
The first is to think that everything comes down to whether one specific answer was right or wrong. But what you bought was not an answer. It was the continued guidance the service offers.

The second is to treat the case as a simple software license agreement, as if you had installed a program on your computer. That hides the fact that the service changes all the time, and that the one changing it is the company.
The first is to treat the conflict as a mere dispute over an isolated factual error, as if the usefulness of the service came down to the abstract correctness of each individual answer.<1>p. 757</1>
Neither reading reaches the central problem.<1>p. 757</1>
How does the problem usually show up?
<1>When the answer seems more certain than it is.</1> The text comes well written, organized and confident, and gives an impression of certainty that the service cannot back up.
<1>When you cannot understand what happened.</1> You do not know why you got that answer, whether the service changed its behavior or what influenced the result that guided your decision.
<1>When all the evidence stays with the company.</1> The history, the context of the conversation and the internal records are with whoever provides the service, and not with you.

None of this needs to be an outright lie to count. It is enough that the service trades clarity for an appearance of confidence and leaves you alone with the cost of the error, the change or the loss.

There may be functional opacity when the user cannot reconstruct, in minimally verifiable terms, why a given output was presented to them, to what extent there was a relevant change in the system's behavior or which elements of the environment conditioned the answer that guided their conduct.<1>p. 759</1>
In these scenarios, the injury need not appear as an outright lie to be legally relevant.<1>p. 759</1>

It is enough that the environment replaces legibility with a performance of confidence, shifting to the user the cost of bearing error, revision, fluctuation or functional loss without adequate institutional trails of reconstruction.<1>p. 759</1>

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to trust signals that someone else controls. Here it grows larger, because you depend on the assistant to understand things and have no way of checking the signals that the answer is good, complete and sufficient.

It is semiotic vulnerability intensified by epistemic dependence, that is, by subjection to an environment that administers the signs of the reliability, usefulness and sufficiency of the answer without granting the recipient, to the same extent, means of verification and audit.<1>p. 758</1>
A wrong answer, on its own, says little. What counts is reconstructing the whole path.
The conversation history, with the questions and the answers.
The context in which you used the service.
The warnings that appeared or were missing.
The way the answer was presented.
The role the answer played in your decision.
Save what you can while it is still accessible, such as screenshots, exported conversations and dates.
Which traps make you give up too early?
<1>Thinking the problem is only the sentence.</1> The sentence convinced you because the whole service was built to look reliable, and that counts too.
<1>Thinking the warning that the system can make mistakes settles everything.</1> A generic warning is not enough, on its own, to rule out any problem with the information you received.
<1>Thinking the variation is a technical matter, like changing weather.</1> The assistant's behavior is governed by the company, and that is why the lack of clarity about it must have a limit.
What must the company guarantee?

No one can demand that the company open its code or show how the system works on the inside. But in a service made to guide you, it must guarantee a minimum that makes it possible to check what happened.

Depending on the case, this includes keeping the history accessible, keeping minimal records of the conversation and stating clearly the limits that really matter. It also includes giving understandable notice when the rules of use change and making it possible to reconstruct the link between what the service promised and the effect it had.
Without this, the company holds two powers at once. The power to guide you and the power to decide on its own what can be told and proven when the guidance fails.

This includes, depending on the case, preservation of accessible history, minimal traces of interaction, sufficient disclosure of materially relevant limits, intelligibility regarding changes in the regime of use and the possibility of reconstructing the link between the functional promise of the service and the impact produced on the user's experience.<1>p. 759</1>

Without this, the platform retains not only the power to provide guidance, but also the power to define unilaterally what may be narrated and proven when that guidance proves inadequate, inconsistent or harmful.<1>p. 759</1>

The most fitting response is usually to correct what failed, and not only to pay for the damage. It may be possible to ask for records that can be checked, for the company to review the way the service communicates and for the lost trust to be restored.

In the most serious cases, when the service repeatedly exploits your trust without giving means to check and contest, the very purpose of the design may come into question. This applies above all when the lack of clarity is not a technical leftover but a stable part of the way the service makes money.
How do you know if this is your case?
Answer for yourself.
Did you use the service to make decisions or to work, and not just out of curiosity?
Did the quality, the behavior or the rules change without a clear explanation?
Are you unable to reconstruct what happened without the company's records?
Did the change have a concrete effect on what you did or lost?
The more yes answers, the more your case resembles what the law protects here. This does not guarantee the outcome, but it shows where to start.
Enjoyment, here, must be read as governed cognitive enjoyment.<1>p. 758</1>
